bullets: Three variables to explain: output Y, unemployment u, inflation π. The interest rate r connects them.
GDP three ways, same answer: final goods produced, value added (final output − intermediate consumption), incomes (wages + profits).
Nominal GDP = Σ P_t·Q_t (current prices). Real GDP = Σ P_0·Q_t (base-year prices): only quantities move it.
Nominal growth ≈ real growth + inflation. Cars example: +10% = 0% + 10%. The base year is a choice.
GDP per capita = GDP / population. GDP measures output, not well-being or distribution.
Unemployment: L = N + U, u = U/L. Must be without work, looking and available; people who stop looking leave L, so u can fall while the labour market worsens.
CPI = Σ(P_t·Q_0) / Σ(P_0·Q_0) × 100 (fixed basket). Deflator = nominal GDP / real GDP × 100. π = (P_t − P_t−1)/P_t−1.
Falling inflation is not falling prices: prices fall only under deflation. Short run demand decides output; medium run capacity does.
examTip: Classic traps: confusing inflation falling with prices falling, and dividing the wrong way round for the deflator (nominal / real × 100).

session: Session 2 - Topic 1: Output, consumption, investment and the multiplier
bullets: Expenditure approach: Y = C + I + G + X − IM. Imports are inside C, I, G so they are removed once at the end. Transfers and interest are not in G.
Investment = newly produced capital (fixed non-residential, residential, inventory). Shares and resold houses are not investment.
Aggregate demand Z = C + I + G (X = IM = 0 for now). Y − Z = unplanned investment.
Consumption function C = c0 + c1·YD, YD = Y − T, 0 < c1 < 1 (MPC). Change in YD: move along the line; change in c0: the line shifts.
MPC + MPS = 1, APC + APS = 1. APC = c1 + c0/YD falls towards MPC. Saving S = −c0 + (1 − c1)YD, threshold YD* = c0/(1 − c1).
NPV = −cost + Σ CF_t/(1 + r)^t. Invest if NPV > 0, equivalently IRR > r. Higher r lowers present values.
Investment curve I = I0 − e·r: change in r moves along it, change in I0 shifts it. Accelerator: net investment IN = ΔK depends on ΔY, so I is volatile.
Multiplier = 1/(1 − c1). With c1 = 0.6 it is 2.5: ΔI = 100 gives ΔY = 250 (100 + 60 + 36 + ...). It is finite only because c1 < 1.
examTip: Use YD (not Y) in the consumption function, and separate the multiplier (a number) from the output effect (in dollars); shift vs movement along is tested constantly.

session: Session 3 - Topic 1: Equilibrium, fiscal policy, deficits and debt
bullets: Equilibrium Y = Z. Y > Z: stock piles up, firms cut output. Y < Z: shelves empty, firms produce more. Three look-alike equations: identity, Z definition, condition Y = Z.
Output can settle below full-employment output Y_FE: a negative output gap. Above it: a positive gap and rising prices.
Government spending multiplier 1/(1 − c1) = 2.5. To close a gap of 150 you need ΔG = 60. Tax multiplier = −c1/(1 − c1) = −1.5, so ΔT = −100 for the same 150.
Balanced-budget multiplier = 1 (Haavelmo). Paradox of saving: if all save more, c0 falls, Y falls and saving ends unchanged (S = I − (T − G)).
Taxes with income T = T0 + tY: multiplier 1/(1 − c1(1 − t)) = 1.82 with t = 0.25. Automatic stabilisers dampen shocks.
Debt: D_t = (1 + r)D_t−1 + (G − T). Primary deficit = G − T. Debt ratio climbs by itself if r > g and falls if g > r.
Exits from unsustainable debt: primary surplus, default (haircut), monetary financing (inflation). Spread rising with r can create a doom loop.
examTip: Tax cuts have a smaller multiplier than spending (households save part first); remember the first-round size is c1 times the tax change.

session: Session 4 - Topic 2: Money, bonds and the interest rate
bullets: Money = what you can pay with (cash and deposits); income is a flow; wealth is everything owned minus owed. A savings account is not money here.
Real rate r ≈ i − πe. With prices fixed, πe = 0 so r = i.
One-year bond price P_B = 100/(1 + i); yield i = (100 − P_B)/P_B. Price and interest rate move in opposite directions. Perpetuity price = payment / i.
Money demand Md = $Y × L(i): rises with nominal income $Y, falls with i. Motives: transactions, precautionary, speculative. Example L(4%) = 0.30.
Change in i: movement along money demand. Change in $Y (price level or output): the line shifts. $Y = P × Y.
Money market: M = $Y × L(i). Central bank buys bonds (open market operation): M rises, i falls. It sells bonds to raise i.
Modern central banks set the rate and let M adjust; banks create most money by lending. The floor at zero rate is the liquidity trap.
Long rates ≈ average of expected short rates + risk premium. Two-year 4.25% = average of 4.0% and 4.5%.
examTip: Compute yield on the price paid: (100 − 94)/94, not divided by 100; and know which changes shift the money demand line versus move along it.

session: Session 5 - Topic 3: Unemployment, the labour market and the first Phillips curve
bullets: Counting: L = N + U, u = U/L. Discouraged workers are outside the labour force. Vacancies and unemployment coexist because matching takes time.
Wage setting: W = Pe·F(u, zw). Higher u lowers the wage; higher zw (benefits, minimum wage, protection) raises it. With Pe = P the real wage W/P = 1 − 5u + zw in the example.
Price setting: P = (1 + m)W so W/P = 1/(1 + m), here 0.8 with m = 0.25. It does not depend on u: a flat line.
Natural rate un: where wage and price setting cross (1.2 − 5u = 0.8 gives u = 8%). Not zero because zero unemployment would push wage claims above what firms pay.
Higher zw or higher markup m raises the natural rate. Move the right line, then read the new crossing.
Natural output Yn = N_n = L(1 − un). Unemployment above un is cyclical. Example L = 1,250, un = 8% gives 1,150.
Okun's law: growth 1 point above normal lowers u by about 0.4 points (labour hoarding and discouraged workers).
Below un: wages and prices rise. Phillips curve found in 1958; it stops lining up after 1970 (topic 4).
examTip: Draw the real wage W/P (not W) on the vertical axis, and say which line moves (zw shifts wage setting, m shifts price setting).

session: Session 6 - Topic 4: Inflation, expectations and the Phillips curve
bullets: Pay is set on expected prices, so expected inflation feeds wages then prices: π = πe + (m + zw) − αu, equivalently π = πe − α(u − un).
At u = un, π = πe. Below un, inflation comes in above expectations. Example un = 6%, α = 0.5, πe = 2%: at u = 4%, π = 3%.
Expectations: πe = θ·π(t−1) + (1 − θ)·π̄. θ = 0 means anchored, θ = 1 means people expect last year's inflation.
Anchored: unemployment moves the level of inflation (1960s, and since mid-1990s, flatter). De-anchored (1970s to 1995): accelerationist curve, inflation keeps rising below un.
NAIRU: the u at which inflation does not change. In the model it equals un. Long-run Phillips curve is vertical at un: no lasting trade-off.
Sacrifice ratio = 1/α = 2: one point less inflation needs two point-years of u above un.
Central banks target inflation (π* = 2% for the ECB and the Fed) with the policy rate. A positive target leaves room to cut rates and avoids forcing pay cuts.
Supply shock such as energy: m rises, so inflation and the natural rate rise. Dilemma: raise rates and risk jobs, or wait and risk expectations de-anchoring.
examTip: Do the arithmetic with u − un in percentage points, and say whether inflation is above or below what was expected before saying anything about the level.

session: Session 7 - Topic 5: The IS-LM-PC model (closed economy)
bullets: Real cost of a loan: r ≈ i − πe (Fisher). Borrowers compare what an asset earns with the interest paid. Prices fixed today: r = i.
Investment I = I0 − e·r; example I = 200 − 20r. A lower rate raises I, then output via the multiplier 2.5.
IS: Y = 2.5 × (480 − 20r) = 1,200 − 50r. Each point off the rate adds 50 of output. IS slopes down and shows goods-market clearing for each r.
Rate change: movement along IS. G, T, c0, I0 changes: IS shifts. Fiscal policy shifts IS.
LM is flat at the rate the central bank chooses (i = ī); r = i = ī when πe = 0. Monetary policy shifts LM. Banks charge a premium above the policy rate.
Shock protocol: which market, shift or move along, direction, new equilibrium, effect on Y, u, π, r.
Policy mix: cut G by 20 lowers Y by 50; the central bank cuts r by 1 point to offset. Deficit falls, output holds.
If the Fed raises its rate: LM up, output down, unemployment up, along IS. Reason: inflation above the 2% target.
examTip: Decide first whether the shock is on an axis variable (move along IS) or something else (shift), then read Y off Y = 1,200 − 50r.
